courseTitle: How IT Teams Work: Agile, Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban & Software Releases

slots.practicalActivity: Using a project you know well (a work task, a school project, or a hypothetical 'build a personal budgeting app'), write out its five Waterfall phases (Requirements, Design, Build, Test, Release) as a numbered list, then re-plan the exact same project as 3 short Agile sprints (1-2 weeks each) with one sprint goal per sprint. Add a 2-3 sentence note on why a requirement discovered wrong in month four would cost far more to fix under the Waterfall version than the Agile one.
slots.deliverable: A one-page written comparison: the same project planned once as 5 Waterfall phases and once as 3 Agile sprints, with a short note on the cost of a late requirement change under each.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a small feature request (e.g. 'add a dark mode toggle' or 'let a user export their data as CSV'). Write it as a real user story in the 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]' shape, with at least 3 specific, checkable acceptance criteria. Then write a short Sprint Planning note naming who would hold the Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developer roles on a 3-person team working this story over a 2-week sprint.
slots.deliverable: One written user story with 3+ acceptance criteria, plus a short sprint-planning note naming who holds each Scrum role for it.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a 5-column Kanban board (on paper, in a spreadsheet, or a free tool like Trello or GitHub Projects) with Backlog, To Do, In Progress, Review, and Done columns. Add at least 8 cards representing realistic IT tasks, give each one a single owner, set a WIP limit of 3 on 'In Progress', and mark one card 'Blocked' with a one-line reason that's outside the owner's control.
slots.deliverable: A built 5-column Kanban board (screenshot or photo) with 8+ owned cards, a stated WIP limit on In Progress, and at least one card marked Blocked with a reason.

slots.practicalActivity: Take one card from your Kanban board (the previous slot) and write out its full journey from Ticket Assigned through Branch Created, Code Review, Merged to QA, UAT Sign-Off, to Deployed, naming who owns each step (developer, QA engineer/test suite, business stakeholder, everyone). Then write one sentence per environment explaining the specific question Dev, QA, UAT, and Production each answer.
slots.deliverable: A step-by-step written trace of one real ticket through Dev to QA to UAT to Prod with an owner named at each step, plus one sentence per environment on the question it answers.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Git if needed, create a new local folder, run `git init`, create a file, then run the real everyday workflow: `git add`, `git commit -m "..."`, create a branch with `git checkout -b`, make a change, commit it on that branch, and (if you have a GitHub account) `git push` it to a new remote repository to open a real pull request. Also create a `.gitignore` that excludes a fake `.env` file you create in the folder, and confirm `git status` never shows it as tracked.
slots.deliverable: A local Git repository with at least 2 commits across 2 branches, a working `.gitignore` excluding a test `.env` file, and (optionally) the same repo pushed to a real GitHub remote with an open pull request.

slots.practicalActivity: For the feature you wrote a user story for earlier, write a complete release checklist: who approves it, what you'd monitor right after it ships, a specific rollback plan, and a short, specific release note (not 'various improvements'). Then write one paragraph choosing a rollout strategy — blue-green, canary, rolling, or feature flag — for this release and justifying why that one fits.
slots.deliverable: A written release checklist (approval, monitoring, rollback plan, release note) for one feature, plus a justified choice of rollout strategy.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending review for How Work Gets Done: take the single user story you wrote earlier in this chapter and trace it completely through the whole chapter's pipeline in one connected write-up — write its acceptance criteria, place it on your Kanban board, move it through Dev to QA to UAT to Prod with an owner at each step, commit it through a real Git branch/pull-request workflow, and close it out with a release checklist and release notes.
slots.deliverable: One combined write-up tracing a single feature from user story through the Kanban board, the SDLC environments, a real Git branch/commit workflow, and a finished release checklist.

slots.practicalActivity: Read the Castlebridge Retail capstone scenario (a sales director wants a dashboard showing revenue by region and by product category, updated automatically) and complete its first checklist item: write at least 3 real user stories covering the revenue-by-region view, the revenue-by-category view, and the automatic daily refresh, each in proper 'As a... I want... so that...' form with specific acceptance criteria — including an acceptance criterion for what happens when a region has zero sales that month.
slots.deliverable: 3 or more written user stories for the Castlebridge Retail capstone, each with specific, checkable acceptance criteria.

slots.practicalActivity: Finish the Castlebridge Retail capstone: build a Kanban board using the user stories from the previous slot, write a short QA test plan with at least one edge case, write a one-paragraph UAT sign-off in the sales director's voice either approving the work or sending back specific feedback, write a short and specific set of release notes, and write up how you'd investigate and communicate a production incident where last month's numbers show zero for one region two days after launch.
slots.deliverable: A completed capstone package: a Kanban board, a written QA test plan, a UAT sign-off paragraph, specific release notes, and a written production-incident investigation-and-communication plan.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can read a real Kanban/Scrum board, write a proper user story with acceptance criteria, place a change correctly in the Dev to QA to UAT to Production pipeline, use the everyday Git branch/commit/push/pull-request workflow, and run one small IT request end to end as user stories, a board, a test/UAT cycle, and real release notes.
